stem: Price discrimination is the practice of

options.content: charging different prices for the same product to different groups
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: charging a price below the cost of production to drive out rivals
options.rationale: That is predatory pricing.

options.content: charging different prices to different customers because costs differ
options.rationale: Cost-related differences are not discrimination.

options.content: setting the same price for every consumer
options.rationale: That is a uniform price.

explanation: Price discrimination charges different prices for the same good to different consumers or groups, for reasons not related to cost.

stem: First-degree (perfect) price discrimination means that

options.content: each consumer pays the maximum he or she is willing to pay
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: different groups are charged different prices in separate markets
options.rationale: That is third-degree discrimination.

options.content: the price depends on the quantity bought by each customer
options.rationale: That is second-degree discrimination.

options.content: the government sets different prices
options.rationale: That is not price discrimination by a firm.

explanation: Each consumer is charged the maximum price he or she is willing to pay, so all consumer surplus goes to the seller.

stem: Which of the following is a condition for price discrimination?

options.content: The firm is a price-taker
options.rationale: A price-taker cannot choose its price.

options.content: Demand has the same elasticity in all markets
options.rationale: Different elasticities are needed.

options.content: Costs are different in each market
options.rationale: Differences in cost are not required and are not discrimination.

options.content: The firm can prevent resale between the markets
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: Markets must be separable, so consumers who pay the low price cannot resell to those who would pay the high price.

stem: A firm practising third-degree price discrimination will charge the higher price in the market where

options.content: demand is more price elastic
options.rationale: That market gets the lower price.

options.content: demand is less price elastic
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: marginal cost is lower
options.rationale: Marginal cost is assumed the same in all markets.

options.content: there are fewer buyers whatever the elasticity
options.rationale: The number of buyers does not decide the price; elasticity does.

explanation: Demand is less elastic there, so a higher price loses fewer customers.

stem: A bus company charges students a lower fare than other adults, and students must show a card. This is an example of

options.content: first-degree price discrimination
options.rationale: That charges each person a different price.

options.content: third-degree price discrimination
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: second-degree price discrimination
options.rationale: That varies the price with the quantity bought.

options.content: predatory pricing
options.rationale: The fare is not below cost to drive out rivals.

explanation: Different groups in separate markets are charged different prices: third-degree price discrimination, with the card keeping the markets separate.

stem: An electricity company charges more per unit at peak hours than off peak because it must use costly extra generators at peak hours. This is

options.content: price discrimination, because prices differ over time
options.rationale: Discrimination requires price differences not based on cost.

options.content: first-degree price discrimination
options.rationale: Consumers are not charged their maximum willingness to pay.

options.content: not price discrimination, because the price reflects cost
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: predatory pricing
options.rationale: Peak pricing is not aimed at removing rivals.

explanation: The price difference reflects a difference in the cost of supply, so it is not price discrimination.
hints: Is the price difference linked to cost?

stem: Price elasticity of demand is −1.5 in the adult market and −2.5 in the student market for a theatre. To maximise profit the theatre should

options.content: charge students a higher price than adults
options.rationale: Demand is more elastic among students.

options.content: charge both groups the same price
options.rationale: Different elasticities make discrimination profitable.

options.content: charge students a lower price than adults
options.rationale: Correct.

options.content: charge adults a lower price than students
options.rationale: Adults have the less elastic demand.

explanation: Demand is more elastic among students, so a lower price there gains many customers; the less elastic adult market is charged more.
hints: Which market has the more elastic demand?

stem: Price discrimination is most likely to benefit consumers as a whole when it

options.content: reduces the output of the firm
options.rationale: Lower output is a cost to consumers.

options.content: transfers all consumer surplus to the firm in every market
options.rationale: That harms consumers.

options.content: is used only against consumers with no alternative
options.rationale: A captive group is a strong case against discrimination.

options.content: lets the firm serve consumers who would be priced out at a single price
options.rationale: Correct.

explanation: If discrimination lets a firm serve a group that a single price would price out, output rises and more consumers are served.
hints: Think about who may be served only because of discrimination.

stem: A fictional cinema has a constant marginal cost of US\$10 per seat. Demand from adults is P = 58 − 2Q (MR = 58 − 4Q), where Q is the number of seats in hundreds. Calculate the profit-maximising number of seats (hundreds) sold to adults.
explanation: 58 − 4Q = 10 gives Q = 12 hundred seats.
hints: Set MR = MC in the adult market.

stem: Student demand for the cinema is P = 26 − 2Q (MR = 26 − 4Q). Marginal cost is US\$10. Calculate the price charged to students, in US\$.
hints: Find Q from MR = MC, then read the price from the demand curve.

stem: The cinema sells 12 hundred seats to adults at US\$34 and 4 hundred seats to students at US\$18. Calculate its total revenue, in US\$ hundred.
explanation:
1. Adults: 34 × 12 = 408.
2. Students: 18 × 4 = 72.
3. Total revenue = 408 + 72 = US\$480 hundred.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Adults: 34 × 12 = 408.
2. Students: 18 × 4 = 72.
3. Total revenue = 408 + 72 = US\$480 hundred.
hints: Revenue = price × quantity in each market.

stem: If the cinema could practise first-degree price discrimination in the adult market (demand P = 58 − 2Q, marginal cost US\$10), it would sell until price equals marginal cost. Calculate its profit (before fixed costs) in US\$ hundred.
explanation: Output: 58 − 2Q = 10 gives Q = 24. Profit is the triangle between the demand curve and MC: ½ × (58 − 10) × 24 = US\$576 hundred. A single price would give only (34 − 10) × 12 = 288.
workedSolution: 1. Output: 58 − 2Q = 10 gives Q = 24. Profit is the triangle between the demand curve and MC: ½ × (58 − 10) × 24 = US\$576 hundred. A single price would give only (34 − 10) × 12 = 288.
hints: Perfect discrimination: sell until price falls to MC; profit is the triangle between demand and MC.

stem: A firm that is a price-taker can practise price discrimination.
explanation: False. Price discrimination requires market power: the firm must be able to choose its price.

stem: Match each type of price discrimination with an example.

right.content: Cheaper tickets for students and pensioners
Higher prices at peak times because of higher costs
Each buyer pays what he or she is willing to pay in an auction or negotiation
A lower unit price for each extra block of electricity used

explanation: The last example reflects cost, so it is not discrimination.

stem: Complete the statement.

payload.template: To maximise profit a discriminating firm sets {{blank:a}} equal to marginal cost in {{blank:b}} market.

explanation: MR = MC in each separate market.

stem: What word describes the resale of a product by those who buy it at the low price to those in the high-price market?
explanation: Seepage (arbitrage) must be prevented for discrimination to work.

stem: State **three** conditions necessary for price discrimination.

points.description: The firm must have market power (be a price-maker).
The markets must be separable (no resale between them).
Price elasticity of demand must differ between the markets.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The firm must have market power so that it can set its price; the markets must be kept apart so that buyers cannot resell; and the price elasticity of demand must be different in the different markets.

explanation: Three conditions.

stem: Explain why a firm practising third-degree price discrimination charges a lower price in the market with the more elastic demand.

points.description: With more elastic demand a price cut raises quantity by a larger percentage.
So the price cut raises revenue.
The firm sets MR = MC in each market, which gives a lower price where demand is more elastic.
Where demand is less elastic a higher price loses fewer customers, so the price is higher.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In the market with elastic demand, a lower price leads to a larger percentage rise in quantity, so revenue increases. The firm sets marginal revenue equal to marginal cost in each market, which gives a lower price where demand is more elastic. Where demand is inelastic a higher price loses few customers, so the firm charges more.

explanation: MR = MC in each market gives a price that depends on elasticity.

stem: Assess the effects of price discrimination on consumers.

points.description: Consumers in the low-price market pay less and some can now buy.
Consumers in the high-price market pay more.
The firm gains more consumer surplus; perfect discrimination removes it all.
Profit may fund a service that would not exist otherwise (cross-subsidy), and output may rise.
Judgement.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Consumers in the low-price market, such as students, pay less and some are able to buy who otherwise could not, while consumers in the high-price market pay more. The firm gains consumer surplus, and under perfect discrimination all of it. However, the extra profit may keep a service in operation, such as a rural route, and output may rise if new consumers are served. Overall, discrimination benefits some groups and harms others; it is more favourable to consumers when output rises.

explanation: Winners, losers and judgement.

stem:
A fictional minibus company in Masvingo serves two groups. Its marginal cost is a constant US\$10 per passenger. Q is in hundreds of passengers and P in US\$ (illustrative data).

| Market | Demand curve | Marginal revenue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adults (A) | P = 46 − 2Q | 46 − 4Q |
| Students (B) | P = 30 − 2Q | 30 − 4Q |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the fare charged to adults when profit is maximised, in US\$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of student passengers (in hundreds).

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Which group has the more price elastic demand at the profit-maximising fares?

options.content: Adults
options.rationale: Adults are charged the higher fare because their demand is less elastic.

options.content: Both groups equally
options.rationale: The fares differ because the elasticities differ.

options.content: Neither, because demand is a straight line
options.rationale: Elasticity changes along a straight-line demand curve.

options.content: Students
options.rationale: Correct: PED is about −2.0 for students against about −1.56 for adults.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain **two** conditions that the company needs to maintain this pricing.

points.description: Market power: the company can choose its fares (no close competitors on the route).
Separation of the markets: students must show a card so adults cannot buy cheap tickets.
Different elasticities of demand (students are more price sensitive).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The company needs market power, so that it can set fares rather than accept a market price. It also needs to keep the markets apart, for example by checking student cards, so that adults cannot buy the cheap tickets.

explanation: Adults pay US\$28 (9 hundred); students pay US\$20 (5 hundred); students' demand is more elastic.
hints: Read each price from its own demand curve.

stem: The minibus company in the previous item has two groups: adults (P = 46 − 2Q) and students (P = 30 − 2Q), with marginal cost of US\$10 and Q in hundreds of passengers. If it charged the same fare to everyone, the combined demand would be P = 38 − Q (for fares below US\$30), giving MR = 38 − 2Q.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the single fare that maximises profit, in US\$.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate profit (before fixed costs) at the single fare, in US\$ hundred.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: With separate fares of US\$28 (9 hundred adults) and US\$20 (5 hundred students), calculate profit before fixed costs, in US\$ hundred.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in profit from discrimination, to one decimal place.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Assess who gains and who loses when the company moves from a single fare to separate fares.

points.description: The company gains: profit rises by US\$16 hundred.
Adults lose: fare rises from US\$24 to US\$28 and passengers fall from 11 to 9 hundred.
Students gain: fare falls from US\$24 to US\$20 and passengers rise from 3 to 5 hundred.
Total passengers are unchanged at 14 hundred; judgement on overall welfare.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The company gains because profit rises from US\$196 hundred to US\$212 hundred. Adults lose, because their fare rises from US\$24 to US\$28 and their numbers fall from 11 to 9 hundred. Students gain, because their fare falls from US\$24 to US\$20 and their numbers rise from 3 to 5 hundred. The total number of passengers stays at 14 hundred, so there is no overall gain in output, and whether the change is desirable depends on how society values the benefit to students against the loss to adults.

explanation: Single fare US\$24 gives profit 196; discrimination gives 212 (+8.2%); adults lose, students gain, total passengers unchanged.
hints: Compare total profit under the two pricing policies.

stem: Assess whether price discrimination is in the interests of consumers.

points.description: Consumers in the low-price market pay less and more of them can buy.
Consumers in the high-price market pay more.
The firm captures consumer surplus; perfect discrimination removes all of it.
Output may rise if previously unserved consumers are served.
Supernormal profit may fund investment or cross-subsidise a loss-making service.
A firm with market power may use discrimination against groups with no alternative.
Competition law or regulation may limit the practice.
A justified judgement.

levels.descriptor: Two-sided, applied and developed, with a justified conclusion.
Some development of one side, limited application or conclusion.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Price discrimination helps consumers in the low-price market, who pay less and, in some cases, can buy at all, such as students on a bus route. It harms those in the high-price market, who pay more than a single price would require, and the firm captures more of the consumer surplus. If discrimination lets the firm serve consumers who would otherwise be priced out, output rises, and the extra profit can fund investment or keep a loss-making service open. But if the firm charges a higher price to a captive group, such as patients, the effect is harmful. Overall, discrimination is more likely to benefit consumers as a whole when it increases output and when the high-price group has alternatives; otherwise it mainly transfers surplus to the firm.

explanation: Winners, losers and conditions for a favourable outcome.
hints: Consider winners and losers, and efficiency.
